chapters.title: Chapter 4: Strategy Sensitivity and Break-Even Analysis

lessons.title: Holding Period, Turnover, and the Cost Drag Formula

children.text: Lesson 1 expressed cost drag in terms of turnover ratio, a number you measure after the fact from a trade log. Turnover ratio is not, however, what most strategy designs actually specify. A rulebook says things like "exit after 15 trading days" or "hold until the signal reverses." This lesson translates cost drag into that language, holding period, so it becomes something you can reason about while designing a strategy, not only after backtesting one.
Turnover and Holding Period Are Two Views of the Same Thing

For a fully invested strategy that continuously rotates positions, replacing the entire portfolio once every H trading days means it does roughly 250 divided by H replacements a year, using 250 as the approximate number of NSE trading days annually. Replacements per year is exactly what turnover ratio measures. The two are the same idea, read in opposite directions.

body.caption: T: annual turnover ratio. H: average holding period, in trading days. 250: approximate NSE trading days per year.

children.text: Invert the turnover ratios from Lesson 1's five strategy archetypes and each one maps to an implied average holding period.

body.caption: Lesson 1's strategies, restated as holding periods

children.text: Cost Drag, Restated in Terms of Holding Period

Substitute T = 250 / H into Lesson 1's cost drag formula and holding period drops straight into the driver's seat: cost drag is inversely proportional to how long you hold. Halve the holding period, trade twice as often, and cost drag doubles. Double the holding period and cost drag is cut in half.

body.title: Cost Drag vs Holding Period (0.30% Round-Trip Cost)

children.text: Solving for the Holding Period a Strategy Needs

Rearranged, the same formula answers a design question directly: given a round-trip cost and a maximum cost drag you are willing to accept, what is the shortest average holding period the strategy can afford?

body.caption: Example: at a 0.30% round-trip cost, capping cost drag at 2% of capital a year requires an average holding period of at least 37.5 trading days, about 7.5 weeks.

body.label: Minimum Holding Period for a 2% Cost Budget
body.context: At a 0.30% round-trip cost. Hold shorter than this on average, and cost drag exceeds 2% of capital a year.

body.text: This is a far more useful check to run before writing a single line of strategy code than after. If a trading idea only works on a 5-day average holding period, this formula says it needs to clear roughly 15% of cost drag a year just to break even on costs, before any allowance for the gross edge actually needing to be positive. Many ideas that look interesting on paper simply cannot survive their own intended holding period, and this formula tells you that in one line, without running a single backtest.

children.text: Why Holding Period Beats Turnover Ratio as a Design Tool

Turnover ratio is measured after a backtest runs, it is an accounting summary of trades that already happened. Holding period is something you actually decide while writing entry and exit rules, whether that is a fixed exit after N days, a trailing stop, or a signal-reversal exit that averages out to some typical duration. Framing cost sensitivity around holding period means you can ask the question that matters at design time: given what this strategy costs to trade, how long does it need to hold a position to be worth building at all?

body.caption: Converting between holding period, turnover, and cost drag

body.title: Quick Check
body.prompt: A strategy's round-trip cost is 0.50%, and you want to keep annual cost drag under 2.5%. What is the shortest average holding period, in trading days, that satisfies this?
body.explanation: H_min = 250 x 0.50 / 2.5 = 50 trading days. Any strategy holding positions for less than about 50 trading days on average, roughly 10 weeks, would push cost drag above the 2.5% budget at this round-trip cost.

body.text: Turnover ratio and holding period are the same relationship seen from two directions, and cost drag is inversely proportional to holding period. Before building a strategy around a particular holding horizon, solve for the minimum holding period its round-trip cost demands, it is a one-line check that can rule a trading idea out before a single backtest is run.

points: Annual turnover ratio and average holding period are inverses of each other: T = 250 / H, using 250 as approximate NSE trading days per year.

Because cost drag equals turnover times round-trip cost, and turnover equals 250 divided by holding period, cost drag is inversely proportional to holding period: halve the holding period and cost drag doubles.
Rearranging the formula gives a minimum viable holding period for a given cost budget, for example about 37.5 trading days at a 0.30% round-trip cost and a 2% annual cost drag limit.

Holding period is a design-time lever, set directly by entry and exit rules, while turnover ratio is only measurable after a backtest has already run, making holding period the more useful frame for deciding whether a strategy idea is worth building at all.
